title: Peter weeps bitterly (Matthew 26:57–75)
hook: a trial inside, a servant girl outside, and Peter's own voice gives him away
tomorrow: Judas brings the silver back. what do they say to him?

segments.voice: A garden, three friends asleep, and a small request: one hour. Then everyone ran, just as he said they would. One of them follows at a distance.

Split screen, like a series cutting between two rooms. Inside the house of Caiaphas the high priest, Jesus is on trial. Outside in the courtyard, Peter, who followed afar off, sits with the servants to see how it ends. Two rooms, two men, and in both of them the same question: who are you, really? Inside, false witnesses come and go. "But Jesus held his peace." Under oath he answers once: "Thou hast said." Outside, a servant girl looks at Peter: "Thou also wast with Jesus of Galilee."
screen: `SPLIT SCREEN.` → `INSIDE: JESUS HELD HIS PEACE.` → `OUTSIDE: THOU ALSO WAST WITH HIM.`

segments.voice: Peter: "I know not what thou sayest." Another maid says the same, and he swears: "I do not know the man." Then the bystanders: "Surely thou also art one of them; for thy speech bewrayeth thee." His way of talking gives him away. He curses and swears again. "And immediately the cock crew. And Peter remembered the word of Jesus... And he went out, and wept bitterly." So what are tears like his for? Christians answer in two ways, and both have a real case. One view: sorrow like Peter's is holy, worth staying in. Its case: a failure taken lightly will happen again, and the psalm says, "a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise." Peter doesn't explain himself or blame the girl. He goes out and weeps, and some Christians see that as the honest beginning of turning around. The other view: don't stay in the tears; the turning point is grace, not how hard you cry. Its case: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins." Sorrow that never looks up for forgiveness can turn into despair, and the person stays stuck. Both views agree on one thing in this scene: Matthew doesn't hide Peter's worst night. He tells it in full, and he ends the chapter on his tears.
screen: `I DO NOT KNOW THE MAN.` · `THY SPEECH BEWRAYETH THEE.` · `VIEW ONE: STAY IN THE SORROW.` · `VIEW TWO: LOOK UP TO GRACE.` · then, large: `HE WEPT BITTERLY.`

segments.voice: On a piece of paper, write one failure in a single plain line, the kind of thing you'd rather nobody knew. Read it once, slowly, without explaining it away. Then fold the paper and hold it in a closed hand while you breathe, letting it be as heavy as it is, no heavier and no lighter.
Peter weeps bitterly. The end of the night Peter denied Jesus three times, and the moment the cock crowed and he remembered.
Hold onto this: he wept bitterly, and Matthew wasn't ashamed to tell it. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some churches read Peter's denial in Holy Week, and in some Christian art Peter is shown beside a rooster, a reminder of this night; some Christians bring failures like his to confession or to prayer.

fork.setup: your friend blew it badly. she says: crying about it is pointless, just move on. you agree with her. what's the best case for the other side?
options: honest sorrow takes the failure seriously; God won't despise a broken heart.
feeling awful for long enough pays off what you did.
tears prove you were a good person all along.
fork.reveal: the sorrow view rests on Psalm 51:17 and on Peter, who doesn't explain himself but goes out and weeps. the grace view rests on 1 John 1:9. Christians hold both.

original.note: Greek: bitterly; how Peter wept in Matthew 26:75.

trapdoor: what you thought: Peter's denial proves he was a coward.
what it means: Matthew sets Peter's lies beside Jesus' silence, and ends the scene on Peter's tears, not his excuses.

what a scholar hears: πικρῶς, bitterly; Matthew intercuts the trial and the courtyard (26:57–75), and Christians debate whether to dwell in such sorrow (Psalm 51:17) or move swiftly to grace (1 John 1:9).

chat.meaning: Peter didn't excuse himself; he went out and wept. Christians see honest sorrow as a start, and grace as what comes after it.

notes: Debate shape: two Christian views on what sorrow over failure is for (stay in it, Psalm 51:17; move to grace, 1 John 1:9), each with its best case, ranking neither. These are broad attitudes, not named church positions; a Keeper should confirm they are fair and recognizable.
The voice abridges 26:75 with '...' between 'the word of Jesus' and 'And he went out'; the full verse is in sources and the myth reveal. Confirm.
The trial is told briefly, with no blame on Jewish people as a whole; the council's verdict and the mocking (26:65–68) are left out. Confirm.
'His way of talking gives him away' explains 'thy speech bewrayeth thee' (26:73); Matthew doesn't say what about his speech. Kept general on purpose.
'Outside in the courtyard' renders 26:69 ('sat without in the palace'). Matthew mentions no fire; the 1479 teaser was written to match.
